transcript.text: Hi Ishaan, good to meet you. I'm part of the team hiring for this role, and today I'd like to hear about your experience in some depth. We have about 15 minutes, and I'll keep time for your questions at the end. What part of your PGP at IIM Ahmedabad has been most engaging so far?
transcript.why: This was a warm-up question to help you settle in. It isn't part of the feedback.

transcript.text: Hi thank you so much for having me here um so actually for me the most engaging part of my PGP at IIM Ahmedabad has been the case-based learning approach like it’s very different from my undergrad because here in almost every class we do real-life cases and discuss them from multiple perspectives so for me um the peer learning happens a lot and I get to hear views from people who have come from very diverse backgrounds not just engineers and also working together in syndicate groups for assignments has really helped me understand how to approach business problems in a structured way and I think that has contributed a lot to my learning actually and I have enjoyed courses like Managerial Economics and Marketing a lot because they are so practical in nature and push us to think about applications rather than just theory
Thanks. Walk me through your career so far, from Asian Paints through your MBA and summer internship.
transcript.why: Your response addressed what you have found engaging in your PGP, so I moved on to your broader career path.

transcript.text:
um sure so I started my career at Asian Paints right after my BTech from IIT Bombay I joined as a production engineer at their Ankleshwar plant in Gujarat so there my main responsibility was running the emulsion section on a shift basis so I used to handle around 35 operators and was responsible for ensuring smooth operations quality and productivity during my time there I was able to raise batch yield from about 92 to 95 percent which was actually through small process improvements and working very closely with the shopfloor team apart from that I led a Kaizen project where we worked on reducing the changeover time of the tinting line and managed to bring it down from 70 minutes to 40 minutes so that really improved our flexibility and throughput we also faced a few industrial relations challenges like there was a contract worker stoppage for three days in 2023 so I had to coordinate with the union and management to help bring a quick resolution I did this role for three years and these experiences really made me interested in the strategic side of business so that’s one of the main reasons I decided to do my MBA at IIM Ahmedabad 

at IIMA I have been exposed to many aspects of business and got involved in various academic and extra-curricular activities I also did my summer internship with Aditya Birla Group in their Group Executive Office as a strategy intern so during my internship I evaluated adjacent growth opportunities for the chemicals business and recommended specialty adhesives as a very promising area which is now going into deeper study within the group I was also responsible for building the business case for a greenfield plant where I developed the IRR model and presented it to the leadership so this internship gave me good exposure to top management thinking and how strategy is formulated at a group level so I think these three experiences have made my profile well rounded and prepared me to transition into a business role now
I see you evaluated business adjacencies during your Aditya Birla Group internship. How did you arrive at the specialty adhesives recommendation?
transcript.why: You described your progression, responsibilities, and several outcomes across Asian Paints, IIM Ahmedabad, and Aditya Birla Group. I’m moving to the strategic recommendation you made during your internship.

transcript.text:
so um actually the process was quite structured so we first identified a long list of potential business adjacencies by looking at trends in the chemicals sector and also aligning with the group’s existing core competencies once we had this list I did a screening based on criteria like market size growth potential entry barriers and also the fit with current manufacturing capabilities of the group after that we deep-dived into three shortlisted areas and for that I did secondary research from industry reports and also spoke to a few industry experts and vendors to get a practical understanding 

when it came to specialty adhesives specifically I noticed strong double-digit demand growth in sectors like packaging automotive and construction plus there was a good overlap with the group’s existing raw materials and process know-how so the entry barriers were moderate and the margins were also attractive compared to more commoditized areas I put together a comparative assessment matrix for the adjacencies and presented it to the leadership and specialty adhesives scored high on future potential synergy and competitiveness so based on that I recommended it for further evaluation which the team accepted and started working more deeply on that area
You presented the recommendation and the team began deeper study. What specifically changed after leadership accepted it?
transcript.why: You explained how you compared the three areas and why specialty adhesives ranked highly. I asked what changed after leadership accepted your recommendation to understand the outcome of your work.

transcript.text: um so actually after leadership accepted the specialty adhesives recommendation what changed was that the project became a higher priority focus area for the group chemicals team so they set up a dedicated internal team to look into the technical feasibility and actually started engaging with potential technology partners and consultants so the market research also became more granular at that point and business development resources were allocated to evaluate possible customer segments and initial go-to-market strategies so basically the group leadership began considering capex and resource allocation for this opportunity which was not the case earlier when it was just one among many adjacencies so yeah that’s all I had on that
What concrete outcome showed that the recommendation had moved beyond an initial proposal?
transcript.why: You described the team’s follow-on work, so I asked what evidence showed the recommendation had progressed beyond an initial proposal.

transcript.text: um so actually the most concrete outcome was when the group chemicals team started discussing the potential project with external technology partners and initiated NDAs for information sharing which showed a real intent to move forward beyond just internal discussion also there was a formal kickoff of a feasibility study involving both technical and commercial aspects with defined timelines and milestones so from that point they had started making preliminary site visits and started evaluating prospective locations for the plant so all these steps were signs that it had progressed from just a proposal stage to actual exploration and due diligence and not just a theoretical idea
Which of the other shortlisted adjacencies did you rule out, and what was the deciding reason?
transcript.why: Your answer established what happened after the recommendation, but not which alternatives you ruled out or why. I asked about the judgment behind that choice.

transcript.text: um so one of the other adjacencies we had looked at was specialty solvents but that was ruled out mainly because the market was already quite fragmented and dominated by established players so the entry barriers were high and also the margins were under a lot of pressure from cheaper imports so it didn’t really make sense for the group to enter another me-too commodity space the other one was high-performance coatings and while that looked attractive on the surface after digging deeper we found that regulatory approvals are very stringent and require significant investment in application technology and certifications so basically the risk-reward ratio was not that favorable compared to specialty adhesives so those were the main reasons why we decided to drop those and focus on adhesives
Let's move to your plant experience. How did you handle the stakeholder situation during the contract-worker stoppage at Asian Paints?
transcript.why: Your answer explained which alternatives were rejected and why, so I moved to another experience involving stakeholder coordination.

transcript.text: um sure so basically during the contract-worker stoppage in 2023 at Asian Paints it was a pretty tense situation because contract workers are essential for our plant operations and the stoppage happened kind of suddenly so my main approach was to act as a bridge between the union committee and plant management so the first thing I did was listen to both sides to really understand their concerns the workers were mainly worried about some changes in shift allocation so I made sure I communicated that clearly to our HR and management team and then I also explained the management’s perspective to the union representatives to avoid any misunderstandings I helped facilitate a series of meetings where both sides could air their issues and I ensured minutes were taken and actions were tracked with deadlines since production was impacted we also had to do contingency planning within the emulsion section like reallocating permanent staff temporarily and prioritizing critical batches during those days I think my focus was mainly on maintaining transparent communication and trying to keep tempers in check and I learned that small proactive steps like checking in regularly with the team and updating everyone on progress really helped build trust so finally after a few rounds of discussion an interim solution was agreed and the workers resumed work before it escalated further so I felt I was able to contribute by being approachable and solution-oriented in that situation
Which decisions or actions in those meetings were personally yours to make?
transcript.why: Your answer described the coordination process and the eventual resolution, but not precisely which decisions were yours. I asked to separate your contribution from the wider team’s response.

transcript.text: um so actually as a production engineer my formal authority was a bit limited but there were a few things which were in my control so I made the call to prepare and share daily progress updates with both plant management and the union committee to ensure everyone had the same information also I decided which production activities to prioritize on the shopfloor during those days like based on raw material availability and delivery schedules I suggested to management that we can temporarily redeploy a couple of skilled permanent operators to fill critical roles in the emulsion section just to keep the essential batches moving apart from that it was mostly about facilitating communication so I made sure the meetings happened on time that the right people were present and that minutes were properly recorded and circulated but the major decisions like shift policy changes or final agreements were taken by senior management and HR so my role was more to enable smooth coordination on the ground and execute whatever immediate operational adjustments were needed to reduce production loss
How did you judge that the situation was moving toward resolution?
transcript.why: You clarified which operational decisions were personally yours. I asked how you judged progress because the outcome was described as resumed work without a specific basis for knowing the situation was improving.

transcript.text: um so actually I judged that the situation was moving toward resolution mainly by observing changes in the tone and willingness of both sides during the meetings like in the first couple of discussions both management and the union were quite rigid but after we facilitated a few open conversations I noticed that there was more flexibility and people started coming up with practical suggestions instead of just repeating demands also the union committee started sharing interim proposals rather than sticking to only their original ask so that was a signal for me that they were open to compromise plus we saw that absenteeism was dropping some workers started coming back to check in at the plant and I noticed the supervisors were able to get more clarity on shift rosters another indicator was that the frequency of meetings and actual follow-up actions improved so both sides began sticking to timelines and we could see progress on small pain points so all these signs together told me that the issue was getting closer to resolution and I just kept focusing on ensuring open communication right till the end

Let's switch to a market-entry question. Suppose a chemicals company is considering entering a new category with limited market data. How would you decide what to investigate before recommending investment?
transcript.why: Your answer explained the signs you used to judge whether the situation was improving, including greater flexibility, returning workers, and completed follow-ups. I moved on after hearing how you personally tracked progress.

transcript.text: um okay so if I was in that situation where a chemicals company wants to enter a new category but market data is limited I think my first step would be to try and identify what the critical unknowns are for the decision so basically I’d want to break down the opportunity into key drivers like market size potential growth rate entry barriers possible customer segments and also how well the company’s existing strengths fit with this new category so since data is limited I would probably start with secondary sources like industry reports trade associations or even government publications to get any base estimates if that’s not enough then I would see if we can do primary research maybe some expert interviews or even targeted discussions with potential customers and suppliers to fill in the gaps another aspect to look at would be competitor activity if there are already incumbents then studying their products pricing and distribution could give signals about entry challenges and market attractiveness I would also try to assess regulatory requirements or technology barriers because those can often be deal breakers in chemicals so essentially my aim would be to focus the investigation on the most decision-critical uncertainties and gather just enough data either qualitative or quantitative to build a directional business case I’d also want to map possible risks up front and suggest how those could be mitigated if the company did go ahead so I think by following a structured approach like this we can make a reasoned recommendation even when data is scarce
You would begin with secondary sources and then use primary research to fill gaps. What would make you choose one source of evidence over another?
transcript.why: Your answer listed several useful sources and factors, but it did not show how you would choose among them when time and data are limited. I asked what would make one source more valuable than another.

transcript.text: um so actually the choice between secondary and primary sources depends a lot on what type of information I am looking for and how reliable or recent the available data is so usually I would prefer to start with secondary sources because they are quicker and often give a good overview like industry reports can tell me about broad market sizes and trends but if I find that specific details like niche customer requirements or recent competitor moves are not covered well or the data seems outdated then I would go for primary research like direct interviews or surveys um I think another factor is data credibility because sometimes secondary sources might be biased or inconsistent so I would use primary sources to cross-check or validate critical assumptions also cost and time are important so if the decision is very high-stakes or there is a big gap in available data then going for primary research makes sense otherwise I’d rely on what’s available so basically it’s about balancing speed depth and reliability depending on how important that evidence is for making the investment decision
